relations.note: Tashmetu and Nabû converse, enter the garden, and undergo ceremonial conjugal seclusion.
relations.source: Love Lyrics of Nabû and Tashmetu

relations.note: The divine couple jointly receives prayers, offerings, dedications, and royal invocations.
relations.source: Royal inscriptions, prayers, seals, and letters

relations.note: Tashmetu and Nabû jointly grant Aššurbanipal understanding and scribal knowledge.
First-millennium genealogy presents the male tutelary god Uraš as Tashmetu’s father.
Tashmetu entered Marduk’s divine court during her Old Babylonian assimilation.
After Nabû became Marduk’s son, learned genealogy made Tashmetu Marduk’s daughter-in-law.
Tashmetu joined the Marduk–Ṣarpānītu circle and appeared with them in royal divine sequences.
relations.source: Sippar evidence and royal divine sequences

relations.note: Tashmetu and Nanaya appear as co-wife, rival, or complementary partners of Nabû.
Shared titles and transferred epithets produced partial, but never complete, identification.
An Old Babylonian letter invokes Ištar and Tashmetu together to bless its recipients.
A late syncretic hymn identifies Tashmetu with Ištar among numerous goddess equations.
Tashmetu occupied an uncertain position within or near Ištar-Aššurītu’s cultic household.
Tashmetu was situated in Aššur’s temple environment, without a surviving narrative encounter.
Anu bestowed hearing, obedience, and reconciliation upon Tashmetu.
A damaged prayer places Dagan within the divine hierarchy surrounding Tashmetu’s passage.
The king escorts Šērūa, Kippat-māti, and Tashmetu together into Anu’s temple.
Kippat-māti accompanies Tashmetu and Šērūa in an Assur temple procession.
Kippat-māti may have displaced Tashmetu in some Assur rituals under Sennacherib.
A proposed equation derives solely from the learned identification of their husbands.
Prayers to Nisaba and Tashmetu share a sequence through Nabû and learned culture.
